Stone Age in India: Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic

The Stone Age in India is the long period when people made tools mainly from stone. It is divided into the Palaeolithic (hand axes and flakes, from well over a million years ago), the Mesolithic (tiny microliths, after the last ice age) and the Neolithic (polished tools, farming and villages, from around 7000 BCE in the northwest).

We run stone tools sessions, prehistory lectures and guided visits to Bhimbetka for schools, colleges and adult groups.

What the Stone Age means

Archaeologists divide the human past by the materials and technologies people used. The Stone Age covers the longest part of the human story, before metal tools came into use. In India it is divided into three broad periods: the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age, the Mesolithic or Middle Stone Age, and the Neolithic or New Stone Age. These stages did not begin and end at the same time everywhere: hunting and gathering continued in some regions long after farming villages appeared in others.

The evidence comes mainly from stone tools, but also from animal bones, plant remains, rock shelters, paintings and burials. Dating relies on methods such as stratigraphy, radiocarbon, luminescence and cosmogenic nuclide dating, explained in our guide to how archaeologists date artifacts. Because the evidence is fragmentary, dates are usually given as approximate ranges.

Palaeolithic: the Old Stone Age

The Palaeolithic in India is usually divided into Lower, Middle and Upper phases. The Lower Palaeolithic is marked by Acheulian tools: large, two-sided hand axes and cleavers, shaped by striking flakes off a stone core. Sites are found across the subcontinent, from the Siwalik hills to Tamil Nadu, with important clusters in the Narmada valley, the Deccan and the eastern coast.

Attirampakkam, near Chennai in Tamil Nadu, is one of the most important. Excavations there produced Acheulian tools dated by cosmogenic nuclide methods to around 1.5 million years ago, among the oldest in South Asia. Later layers at the same site show a shift to Middle Palaeolithic flake tools, dated to roughly 385,000 years ago. Isampur in Karnataka is another key Acheulian site, with a quarry and workshop where tools were made. A partial human skull from Hathnora in the Narmada valley is the best known human fossil of this age from India, though its exact date and classification are debated.

The Middle Palaeolithic brought smaller, carefully prepared flake tools such as scrapers and points. The Upper Palaeolithic saw blades and burins, and early forms of ornament, such as ostrich eggshell beads found at sites in central and western India.

Mesolithic: the age of microliths

The Mesolithic began as the climate warmed after the last ice age. People made microliths: tiny, carefully shaped blades and geometric pieces, often less than a few centimetres long, which were set into wooden or bone handles to make arrows, sickles and knives. This technology suited hunting smaller and faster game, fishing and gathering a wider range of plants.

Important Mesolithic sites include Bagor in Rajasthan and Langhnaj in Gujarat, and Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama in the Ganga plain of Uttar Pradesh, where burials give evidence of people's health and diet. Many rock shelters in central India were used intensively in this period, and much of the earliest rock art is attributed to Mesolithic hunter-gatherers.

Bhimbetka: the long story in one place

Bhimbetka, south of Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh, is a cluster of hundreds of natural rock shelters in the Vindhyan hills, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003. Excavations show occupation from the Acheulian onwards, through the Middle and Upper Palaeolithic, the Mesolithic and later periods, making it one of the best places in India to see the Stone Age sequence.

Bhimbetka is best known for its paintings: hunting scenes, animals, dancers, processions and later horse riders and symbols. Many are attributed to the Mesolithic, while others are much later. A guided visit to Bhimbetka's painted shelters is the clearest introduction to Indian prehistory you can get on site, and our guide to rock art in India puts it in context. Talaash Heritage also runs a lecture on rock art of India for classes who cannot travel.

Neolithic: farming, herding and villages

The Neolithic brought domesticated plants and animals, settled villages, polished stone axes, grinding stones and, in many regions, pottery. It appeared at different times in different parts of the subcontinent, and regional Neolithic cultures differ a great deal.

  • Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan (now in Pakistan), is the earliest well-studied farming settlement in South Asia. From around 7000 BCE its people grew barley and wheat, kept cattle, sheep and goats, and lived in mud-brick houses. Later levels lead towards the Indus civilisation.
  • Burzahom, near Srinagar in Kashmir, has a Neolithic phase from about 3000 BCE with pit dwellings, bone tools, polished stone axes and burials, some with dogs buried alongside people.
  • The southern Neolithic of Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, with sites such as Budihal, Utnur and Sanganakallu, was centred on cattle herding and is known for ash mounds formed from burnt cattle dung.
  • Chirand in Bihar and sites in the Belan valley show Neolithic villages in the middle Ganga region, and the northeast has its own Neolithic with cord-impressed pottery.

Why the Stone Age matters today

The Stone Age covers more than 99% of the human past in South Asia. It shows how people adapted to changing climates, how they spread across the subcontinent, and how farming and villages emerged slowly and in many places rather than in a single moment. For students of anthropology, it also connects archaeology with the study of human evolution and of hunter-gatherer ways of life.

The best way to understand stone tools is to handle them. A stone tools session shows how hand axes, flakes and microliths were made and classified using safe replicas, and a lecture on the move from stone tools to the first villages follows the story from the Palaeolithic to the Neolithic. For those who want a longer immersion, the prehistory field school takes the learning outdoors.

Questions people ask

What are the three phases of the Stone Age in India?

The three phases are the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age, marked by hand axes and flake tools; the Mesolithic or Middle Stone Age, marked by tiny microliths; and the Neolithic or New Stone Age, marked by polished tools, farming, animal herding and settled villages. Their dates differ from region to region.

Which is the oldest Stone Age site in India?

Attirampakkam near Chennai is among the oldest, with Acheulian hand axes dated to around 1.5 million years ago. Isampur in Karnataka and sites in the Siwalik hills are also very early. New research may revise these dates, so treat any single site as the oldest with some caution.

Why is Bhimbetka important for the Stone Age?

Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh has rock shelters used from the Acheulian period through the Mesolithic and later, so one site preserves a long sequence of tools and occupation. It is also famous for rock paintings, many attributed to Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003.

What is special about Burzahom?

Burzahom near Srinagar is a Neolithic site from about 3000 BCE, known for pit dwellings dug into the ground, bone tools, polished stone axes and burials in which dogs were sometimes buried with people. It shows a distinct Neolithic culture in the Kashmir valley.

Is Mehrgarh in India?

No. Mehrgarh is in Balochistan, in present-day Pakistan. It is still central to the study of Indian prehistory because it is the earliest well-studied farming village in South Asia, occupied from around 7000 BCE, and its later levels lead towards the Indus civilisation.
